name: Hoop snake
description: A legendary serpent of North American (and Australian) folklore that grasps its tail in its mouth and rolls like a wheel to chase prey, striking with a venomous stinger on its tail.
full_description: The hoop snake is a legendary creature of North American frontier and lumberjack folklore — and, more sparingly, of Australian folklore — characterised by an unusual mode of locomotion. Rather than slithering, the hoop snake reportedly grasps its tail in its mouth, forms a hoop, and rolls along the ground like a wheel to pursue prey at high speed; at the moment of attack it straightens out and stabs the victim with a venomous stinger on its tail. According to one frequently quoted 1784 letter, the hoop snake 'throws himself into a circle, running rapidly around, advancing like a hoop, with his tail arising and pointed forward.' One distinctive defensive lore: a person attacked by a hoop snake is said to be able to dodge behind a tree, which receives the venomous strike and dies from the toxin, leaving the would-be victim unharmed. The creature is reported across the Eastern and Midwestern United States — particularly Virginia, West Virginia, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and the Carolinas — as well as Prince Edward Island and parts of British Columbia. Naturalist Raymond Ditmars famously offered a standing reward for verified evidence; no specimen has ever been produced. Folklorists and herpetologists generally treat the hoop snake as a tall-tale figure, noting possible inspirations in the rainbow snake (Farancia erytrogramma), mud snake (Farancia abacura), sidewinder rattlesnakes, and the cartwheeling defensive behaviour of the Southeast Asian dwarf reed snake.
origin: Reports cluster in the eastern and midwestern United States and parts of Canada, with Australian parallels.

etymology.origin: American English compound: 'hoop' (a circular band) + 'snake'. Named for the legendary tail-in-mouth wheel form of locomotion.
etymology.meaning: A snake that forms a hoop.
etymology.first_use: Documented in late 18th-century letters; widely circulated in 19th-century American frontier and lumberjack folklore.

timeline.event: Frequently cited 1784 letter describes the hoop snake's hoop-rolling pursuit and venomous tail strike
timeline.significance: Earliest commonly cited written description of the hoop snake
timeline.source: Wikipedia article on the hoop snake (citing 1784 letter)

timeline.event: Henry H. Tryon's Fearsome Critters (Idlewild Press) includes the hoop snake among classic lumberjack fearsome critters
timeline.significance: Codifies the hoop snake within the printed fearsome-critter canon
